summary: Long Island Sound light in the Race off Orient Point, first shown about 1805; the 1869 granite tower stands, automated in 1978, sold at federal auction in 2012.

lens.where: East End Seaport Maritime Museum (removed from the tower in 1995)

structures.note: 81 feet (24.7 m) tall; standing; begun 1867, finished 1869 with stone from the original tower
Original tower, 53 feet above sea level; partly dismantled for the 1869 tower

structures.type: Second Empire keeper's house, granite and wood, mansard roof
structures.note: Destroyed by fire 20 April 1944; one-story replacement removed by the Coast Guard in 2002; concrete slab remains

access.note: Closed; the archive lists it as not open to the public. Sold at federal auction in 2012 to a private buyer (LighthouseFriends). Reached only by boat across the Race; visitors should not land.

events.note: Congress act provides $8,000 for lighthouses and buoys on the Sound (LighthouseFriends)
Government buys the island from Benjamin Jerome for $800
Station goes into operation in 1805 (LighthouseFriends); the archive gives 1806 as established
Original freestone tower; archive year established 1806
A small British force landed on 28 July 1813 and removed the lamps and reflectors for the duration of the war
Great hurricane of 23 September 1815 heavily damaged the lantern and broke the windows; the station took refuge in the tower
Congress appropriates $30,000 for works to preserve the island (27 April 1816)
Circular stone wall about 100 feet across built around the station
Third-order Fresnel lens in the original tower
Granite tower finished (begun 1867), 81 feet (24.7 m) tall; using stone from the original tower; granite keeper's house in Second Empire style
Second-order Fresnel lens first exhibited 15 December 1869
Steam fog signal set up with the new tower; duplicate completed 1872
Propeller steamer Galatea grounded in calm fog on Little Gull Island about one-eighth mile from the fog signal; got off two days later without damage (Johnson). Dated 1880 in the 1893 Board report.
Board investigation of the fog signal after the Galatea grounding; fog-signal audibility tests at the station in 1881, 1885 and 1893
Light fuel changes from whale oil and lard oil to kerosene (LighthouseFriends)
Automatic siren, two 13-horsepower oil engines and compressed air, replaces the steam siren (in use from 21 January 1900)
Light changed to incandescent oil vapor (LighthouseFriends)
April 1913: keepers Murray, Conklin and Collins brought ashore the captain and crew of a schooner that foundered on Little Gull Island Reef
8 February 1918: keepers Murray, Peterson and Roode rescued a man adrift on an ice cake near the station
15 December 1919: keepers Merry and Douglas rescued six persons from barges that had broken adrift and drifted up to the north side of the island
July 1920: keeper's rowboat sank about 100 yards from the light; Mrs. Douglass drowned (LighthouseFriends only; not confirmed in the Bulletin)
Radiobeacon installed; to be placed in commission on 15 May 1928
Electricity replaces the earlier oil vapor light (LighthouseFriends)
Hurricane of 1938 blew outbuildings into the Sound and sent waves to the second floor of the keeper's dwelling (LighthouseFriends only)
Fire of 20 April 1944 destroys the keeper's house and spreads into the tower; the lens is undamaged, the tower refurbished
Station automated; the Coast Guard maintains the beacon and foghorn
Fresnel lens removed from the tower and placed on display at the East End Seaport Maritime Museum
One-story replacement dwelling removed by the Coast Guard; concrete slab remains
GSA auction of the island: starting bid $50,000 (1 May 2012); eight bidders; high bid $381,000 accepted in October 2012 from a private buyer

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's first years are 1804 (Rowlett's directory), 1805 (LighthouseFriends: station went into operation), 1806 (archive: year established) and 1869 (the standing tower). We follow 1805 for the first light, 1806 for the original tower, and 1869 for the granite tower standing now. No primary record for 1804-1806 was found in the local corpus.
Johnson (1889) dates the grounding 12 May 1881; the 1893 Board report gives 1880. Not reconciled: both are cited.
LighthouseFriends puts the island about seven miles northeast of Orient Point; Newsday (14 December 2012) says about eight miles east. Not reconciled; the story states both.
LighthouseFriends counts eight bidders at the 2012 auction; Newsday names six bidders besides the winner, which implies seven in all. Not reconciled; the story states both.

notes_for_editor: Same name, different place: the corpus lists 'Little Gull Island, Michigan' (light and fog signal appropriations 1894-1901, and Michigan entries in the Board reports). That is a different station and is not used. Keepers: the full archive roster (222 lines, roster.py output, including persons whose connection ended after 1960 and the Coast Guard entries) is listed as the archive prints it, with person slugs; the story names only keepers in the public record before 1960 and Bettencourt (1944). The 2012 buyer is not named: he is a private individual who declined publicity to Newsday. First light: 1804 (record, Rowlett), 1805 (LighthouseFriends), 1806 (archive); no 1804-1806 primary found in the corpus, which starts in 1891 for the Board reports. The Galatea date: Johnson gives 12 May 1881; the 1893 report gives 1880; unresolved. Putnam (1917) mentions air whistles at Little Gull in 1852 (horse-power), while LighthouseFriends says there was no fog signal at the station for fifty-one years after 1805; unresolved and not used. The 1913 Bulletin's date is OCR-damaged ('Apr.i.127'); the story says April 1913; the schooner's name is illegible in the scan (not used). The 1918 and 1920 Bulletin passages are OCR-damaged in places; check PDF pages 20 and 4. The 1920 Bulletin spells the keeper Douglas; the archive spells Douglass. The July 1920 drowning rests on LighthouseFriends alone: a Chronicling America search for Little Gull and Douglass in NY papers, 1920, returned nothing. The 1921 Bulletin commendation for Merry (PDF page 35) is cut off at a page break; not used. The 1938 hurricane account rests on LighthouseFriends alone; the 1938 Bulletin's storm lists (PDF page 40) do not name Little Gull among damaged stations, so the damage is unverified. The 1944 fire rests on LighthouseFriends and Newsday; Coast Guard records were not checked. The 1978 automation date rests on Newsday and LighthouseFriends. The 1869 Board report (lens exhibited 15 December 1869) is not in the corpus. The Commissioner volume's keeper lists (Murray, Kendzia, Newman, Petersen, Merry) were not used. Wikipedia is not cited. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the Newsday copy is dated 14 December 2012 (the earlier note said undated). Newsday and LighthouseFriends disagree on the distance (seven miles northeast vs eight miles east) and on the bidder count (eight vs seven); both stated in the story. The 1944 fire wording follows LighthouseFriends ('much of' the house); Newsday says the house was destroyed. The 1891, 1895 (scan 258), 1896 (scan 323) and 1900 (scan 86) Board pages and the Johnson (scan 141) and Putnam (scan 94) pages were checked against the corpus page index. The fog-signal years are now fiscal years. 'Built about 1805 to 1806' was replaced by the two sources' operating dates. The phrase 'reached only by boat' was replaced by LighthouseFriends' 'best seen by boat'. The Douglass name is spelled as the Bulletin (Douglas) in 1919 and as LighthouseFriends and the archive (Douglass) in 1920 and in the archive roster.
